’

PETITIONER

-

JUDGMENT
SANDOMIRSKY J.

July 27, 2012

PREFACE

[
1
]
This is a mobility case. Two capable
and loving parents are divorcing. The mother seeks to return to Indianapolis,
Indiana where she was born and raised. She proposes to return to the United
States to live in close proximity to her parents, sibling and extended family.
Other than her now dysfunctional marriage and the two daughters it spawned, now
ages 8 and 5
½
, she has no connection to Saskatchewan. On the other hand, her husband
was born, raised and educated in Saskatchewan and it is the area of Swift
Current that his family and friends reside. He now wishes to remain in
Saskatchewan.

[
2
]
Both parents are capable and willing
to provide a home which, in all respects, is adequate for the children
’
s needs. Extended family are positive
and supportive to each of the mother and father in their respective locales.
The daughters love and admire both parents and are saddened by the prospects
that they will be separated from one of their parents by many hundreds of miles
if their mother returns to Indianapolis with or without them. This is the
difficult reality of most mobility cases.

[
3
]
After trial, it lies to a judge,
operating in an adversarial system of law, to determine what lies in the best
interests of these children.

[
4
]
The evidence is not highly
conflicted. The law is well propounded. The truly vexing problem is that
lawyers and judges, operating in an adversarial system, are charged with the
duty of resolving these issues. Even with all the legal training and experience
brought to bear in this case, we are not as well trained nor educated in such
weighty matters as are child psychologists, psychiatrists or other social
scientists whose knowledge base and experience better qualify them to the task
at hand.

[
5
]
This case is a prime example of a
judge, in my case with 45 years combined experience as a family law litigator
and family law division judge, being tasked with the ultimate decision of
custody and mobility. Yet in this case a clinical psychologist, highly
experienced in the domain of custody and access, was employed with the
collateral task of providing to the court a child custody assessment.

[
6
]
By agreement between the parents and
their respective counsel, the assessor appeared as the court
’
s witness. Each counsel therefore
agreed that the report of the assessor would be the only assessment to be
entered as evidence. Accordingly, each counsel cross-examined the assessor.

[
7
]
The assessor defended his balanced
report in all respects. He displayed a high degree of professionalism and
competence in the witness box, as he did in preparing his report.

[
8
]
Mr. Stewart administered a
substantial number of clinical, psychometric tests to the parents and children.
The extensive and thorough nature of these tests and the results generated was
greater in number, substance and coverage than any previous case I have dealt
with. Thus, this case highlights a concern which has challenged and troubled me
for years
—
that is, who can better decide where the best interests of children of
divorcing/separating parents lies, the legally trained mind or the
psychologist? As a corollary to this question, is a judge adequately equipped
to evaluate a psychologist
’
s work without having been trained in the discipline of child
psychology? If there were competing psychologists urging different
recommendations upon the court, the task of evaluating which is the more
clinically sound assessment is quite a formidable task for a judge. In this
case one custody access assessment has been jointly commissioned and endorsed
by the parties.

[
9
]
The assessor does not tread upon
judicial turf by saying whether it is or is not in the children
’
s best interests to relocate to
Indianapolis. The assessor expressly states that he respects that that decision
lies exclusively with the court. The assessor presents to the court, for the
court
’
s edification, the results of both
the battery of psychometric tests and information gleaned by interviews with
the children, parents and parents
’
references.

[
10
]
The assessor concludes that it is, in
his professional opinion, in the children
’
s best interests to be ordered into
the primary care of the mother while stopping short of expressing any opinion
on whether the children should relocate to Indianapolis with their mother.

[
11
]
At this juncture I mention that the
mother testified that she would remain in Swift Current if the court would not
allow the children
’
s primary residence to be in Indianapolis.

[
12
]
The court considers the custody access
assessment as but one body of evidence, albeit usually an important component
of the evidence in a mobility and custody trial. The evidence of each parent
and how they present in the witness box is another substantive component of the
trial, indeed, in my opinion the most substantive and telling evidence in a
mobility or any other custody case. Finally, collateral, supporting,
corroborating and character witnesses make up a tertiary level of evidence in
most of these cases.

[
13
]
It certainly is not the function nor
the practice of our courts to rubber stamp the conclusions and/or
recommendations of a custody access assessor. The assessment must be consistent
or compatible with the weight of other evidence. The assessment must be
balanced and have an air of reality in the context of the whole of the evidence
adduced. There have been cases where a custody access assessment bore no
reality to the preponderance of evidence, and consequently, I outrightly
rejected its conclusions and recommendations. However, in other cases, the
custody access assessment was meaningful and realistically compatible to the
weight of evidence and therefore of probative value and assistance. In this
instance, Mr. Stewart
’
s assessment, based largely on clinical testing is the only
professional, scientific and opinion evidence presented to the court.

[
14
]
What is so important to recognize is
that, unlike the ability of a judge in our Canadian courts, a custody access
assessor has the ability to gather evidence of his or her professional
choosing. The assessor is at liberty to pursue the relevant evidence he or she
requires, wherever that evidence may be found. This is the inquisitorial
approach or method of gathering evidence. In court trials, the presiding judge
is given the case which the litigants and their counsel choose and nothing
more. There are however rare instances where the court takes judicial notice of
obvious facts and realities. Unlike a judge, the assessor is not constrained by
the adversarial system nor by the limitations of the rules of evidence. In
these distinctly different ways, the evidence and findings of a custody access
report are derived in a significantly unrestricted or unrestrained manner,
whereas the judge is confined to the evidence presented. In the pursuit of a
child
’
s best interests the difference in
these two paradigms is striking. Yet, at the end of the day, with a custody
access assessment in evidence, a judge has the benefit of both methods of
gathering evidence.

[
15
]
I have found it necessary to preface
this judgment in the foregoing manner because the evidence/information obtained
by the assessor in this case closely comports with the evidence presented at
trial. The mother and father, together with their supporting witnesses, have
given consistent information to both the court and the assessor. The assessor
’
s extensive clinical testing of the
parents and children has significant probative value and I shall refer
extensively to the different tests employed and the results of those tests
throughout this judgment.

THE
MOTHER
’
S CASE

The
Petitioner
’
s Evidence

[
16
]
The petitioner is 39 years of age. Born
in the United States, the petitioner and her family took up residence in
Indianapolis, Indiana when the petitioner was four years old. The petitioner
’
s mother and father continued to
reside in the family home, a 2000 square foot, four bedroom structure, located
on a spacious lot.

[
17
]
The petitioner attended elementary,
middle and high school in Indianapolis. She was a very good student who also
engaged in various sports.

[
18
]
The petitioner has one sibling, an
older brother, who resides in Indianapolis and visits at the family home
approximately once a week for a dinner. The petitioner says she is not
particularly close to her brother.

[
19
]
The petitioner
’
s father is 73 years old. He is a
computer systems analyst. The petitioner described her relationship with her
father as fine and testified that he was always supportive of her endeavours.

[
20
]
The petitioner
’
s mother is 68 years of age. Though a
retired elementary school teacher, she occasionally substitute teaches at times
of her own choosing. The petitioner states her relationship with her mother has
always been great, they share the same sense of humour and talk easily. Like
her father, the petitioner
’
s mother has been supportive of the petitioner throughout her
lifetime. Indeed, the petitioner
’
s mother came to trial and testified
on her daughter
’
s behalf in similar terms.

[
21
]
The petitioner testified she was an
honour roll student and that she worked very hard at school. After her
graduation from high school in 1991 she proceeded to Wittenberg College in
Springfield, Ohio. There she obtained an undergraduate degree majoring in
biology with a minor in music. The petitioner knew at middle school that she
aspired to go to medical school. Her undergrad studies culminated in graduating
after the four year program, in 1995, cum laude, that is with honours.

[
22
]
The petitioner proceeded to enroll in
the Indiana School of Medicine, graduating in May of 1999. To fund her
education the petitioner received a scholarship, worked summers and obtained
student loans. In her final year of medicine, 1999, the petitioner went to West
Central Africa for two months to gain practical experience in a medical clinic
associated with an organization called Serving in Mission (aka SIM). It was on
that trip that she met the respondent. She testified that the respondent was
visiting missionary friends and assisting them with their work.

[
23
]
After the respondent returned to
Saskatchewan, the petitioner and respondent kept in touch with one another.
Their relationship flourished such that the petitioner invited the respondent
to come to her graduation from medical school in May 1999. Later, in July of
1999 the petitioner visited the respondent in Saskatchewan.

[
24
]
The petitioner then embarked upon her
internship year and residency program in family medicine. This course occupied
the next three years of her life ... her residency taken at the University of
Minnesota, situated in Minneapolis.

[
25
]
The petitioner and respondent married
in the summer of 2000. While the petitioner was doing her residency the
respondent worked at landscaping and renovation in the Minneapolis area. The
petitioner recalls that the respondent may have taken a class or two at the
University of Minnesota as well.

[
26
]
In the summer of 2002, the respondent
’
s education leave was completed. He
was obliged to return to Saskatchewan to resume work within the province having
received provincial financing to further his studies towards his Masters Degree
in agriculture. He received that degree in 2003. The respondent had previously
graduated from high school in 1993 and proceeded to the University of
Saskatchewan where he obtained a Bachelor of Science Degree in agriculture in
1997. The petitioner described this obligation to Saskatchewan Water
Corporation as an 18 month
“
return to service
”
. The petitioner claimed that she and
the respondent were devout Christians, though of different denominations
—
the respondent Mennonite and the
Petitioner Methodist. Both were interested in pursuing further missionary work
when they graduated. The petitioner moved to Saskatchewan upon the
understanding and pretense that the respondent would fulfil his obligation of
18 months return to service and thereafter the petitioner and respondent would
embark upon missionary work, likely in Africa.

[
27
]
In August 2002 the petitioner and
respondent purchased the present family home in Swift Current. The respondent
resumed his work as an irrigation agrologist while the petitioner was employed
in a local medical clinic. That fall, in November 2002, the petitioner and
respondent journeyed to Ecuador for approximately 10 days on missionary work.

[
28
]
The move from Indianapolis to Swift
Current represented a cultural shift for the petitioner. Having lived her life
in a major American city with a population in excess of a million people, the
adjustment to a small city like Swift Current was a big change for the
petitioner. The petitioner found the citizens of Swift Current friendly enough.
However, the petitioner had difficulty with the respondent
’
s family and their lifestyle. The
petitioner testified that the expectations she believed the respondent and she
had for their own family and lifestyle were different from those of the
respondent
’
s extended family. This caused difficulty for the petitioner. The
petitioner expected boundaries, especially for her own home. The respondent
’
s family were accustomed to dropping
in unannounced and they expected each other
’
s homes were open to the other.

[
29
]
The petitioner testified that she and
the respondent decided to have a child. Bianca was born October 21, 2003. The
respondent testified the announcement by the petitioner that she was pregnant
shocked him. However, he acknowledged that they had been trying to conceive a
child. The respondent said that he was happy at the prospect of being a father,
but that it was a daunting proposition for him.

[
30
]
The petitioner took one year
’
s maternity leave and assumed the
primary responsibility for the baby. She breast fed her new born and performed
most of the usual maternal tasks. The respondent was still completing his
return to service work on a full time basis. After work he would assist the
petitioner with housework, but the petitioner testified Bianca was
overwhelmingly her responsibility during the first year. The petitioner
testified that the respondent would also assist his parents on their family farm
which was located a half hour
’
s drive from the City of Swift Current.

[
31
]
The petitioner visited Indianapolis on
three occasions during Bianca
’
s first year. The petitioner then returned to her medical
practice on a part-time basis, working 20 hours per week and being on call at
the emergency room. Her clinical hours were Monday to Friday. Money was not an
issue. The petitioner and respondent agreed that the petitioner would spend
more of her time raising Bianca during her infancy. The child grew and mother
says she trained her daughter and introduced her to early learning. To
accommodate the petitioner and respondent
’
s work schedule, they relied upon the
paternal grandparents to care for Bianca in the afternoons.

[
32
]
By the summer of 2005 the petitioner
and respondent had resided in Swift Current for three years
—
twice as long as they had initially
contemplated. The petitioner was becoming disenchanted with the respondent
’
s dominancy as well as the fact that
the petitioner and respondent were not pursuing their intended plan of doing
missionary work abroad. The respondent, on the other hand, was content to
remain in Swift Current and maintain the status quo. The petitioner and
respondent admitted in their evidence that the marriage was deteriorating for
these reasons. The petitioner testified her relationship with her in-laws,
though they were loving people, was overbearing for her.

[
33
]
The petitioner also testified that in
or about 2005/2006 she discovered that the respondent was habitually viewing
pornography on line. The respondent admitted that he had done so for years and
was seeking help. The respondent stated to the custody access assessor that he
felt addicted to viewing pornography. In his own testimony, the respondent said
he partnered in a program of accountability as a means of stopping his viewing
pornography. He knew his wife was upset with him for his self-confessed
addiction and he sought his pastor
’
s assistance. They installed a
computer program called Covenant Eyes which monitored his internet connection
and recorded his viewing habits. That information was accessible to his pastor
as the accountability partner. The respondent told the court that his addiction
means the
“
temptation never goes away and probably will be there forever
”
. He stated he must be disciplined.

[
34
]
Pornography covers a wide spectrum of
behaviour from viewing erotica, which is legal and not uncommon through to the
opposite end of the spectrum of abnormal and depraved behaviour, exploiting
young children and beastiality being examples. This end of the spectrum often
constitutes criminal conduct. At this trial neither counsel explored what type
of pornography the respondent was viewing. This is regrettable for the court
was charged with the question of whether the respondent or the petitioner
should be awarded primary care of their daughters. Access or co-parenting was
an issue, as well as mobility, that is the petitioner
’
s proposal to relocate the girls to
Indianapolis. Neither the petitioner nor respondent nor any supporting
witnesses, including the assessor, pursued the matter of whether the respondent
’
s obsession with pornography was a
defining factor. To the contrary, all evidence presented the respondent as a
good and loving father who would not harm his daughters. Therefore he argued
that he should have significant contact and influence in his daughters
’
lives. Mr. Stewart did opine that
Bianca and then Sophia, as they aged, would inevitably use their own computer
savvy and tap into their father
’
s pornography sites
—
which would be a detrimental
occurrence and not in the children
’
s best interests.

[
35
]
Despite the waning marriage, the
parties had their second child, Sophia, born November 19, 2006. Again the
petitioner took a year
’
s maternity leave. Likewise, the respondent took a similar
year
’
s maternity leave though he could not
attest that the dates entirely corresponded with the same dates that the
petitioner was on maternity leave. He was certain of the fact that there was
some overlap. At this point in time Bianca was attending preschool two hours at
a time, twice a week. The petitioner breast fed Sophia and again was the
primary caregiver in her maternal role. However, the respondent aided with
housework and seeing Bianca to school. The petitioner said the respondent also
remained at his place of employment with the Water Corporation. He assisted his
family with farming and also worked with his brother on a part-time basis.

[
36
]
In 2007 the Water Corporation wanted
the respondent to assume his retired boss
’
position. That would have required a
move to Outlook, Saskatchewan. Neither the petitioner nor the respondent were
prepared to make that move. The respondent then experienced personality and
work related problems with his new boss. His regular job was to be transferred
to Outlook as a consequence. That prompted the respondent to resign in or about
2008-2009 rather than move to Outlook.

[
37
]
The petitioner had returned to
part-time medical practice by the end of 2007  when Sophia was one year old.

[
38
]
The petitioner testified that she
continued to be the parent primarily charged with the children
’
s health issues. The respondent
participated, but acknowledged that mother was the doctor in the family.

[
39
]
Bianca was enrolled in a French
Immersion School. The petitioner and respondent again agreed that the
petitioner would work part time, 20 hours per week, in order to devote more
time in raising the two young girls. She chose to have afternoon clinic hours.
Until the respondent
’
s resignation from the Water Corporation several months
later, the respondent
’
s parents cared for the girls when the petitioner and
respondent were otherwise working and Bianca was not in preschool.

[
40
]
In the fall of 2009 Bianca began Grade
1 and school was a full-time venture. Bianca attended Oman School in the French
Immersion Program.

[
41
]
By the year 2009 the petitioner and
respondent had resided in Swift Current for approximately seven years. They
both testified that their marriage was not going well. The petitioner says
boundary issues were not being maintained between the parties
’
home and the respondent
’
s family. The petitioner testified
that she felt
“
trapped
”
and
“
controlled
”
and had no autonomy in her own home. She complained her
mother-in-law was intrusive and that she, the petitioner was powerless to stop
her mother-in-law
’
s interference. The petitioner opined that the respondent was
perhaps oblivious as to how much the petitioner resented his family
’
s overbearance. The petitioner
suggested moving away from Swift Current but the respondent insisted that they
must first save a million dollars, or wait until the girls had completed high
school. The respondent also suggested to the petitioner that she might not like
living overseas in the primitive lifestyle of being a missionary in Niger.

[
42
]
By the fall of 2009 there was talk of
divorce and the petitioner and respondent sought marriage counselling. A lawyer
was consulted by the petitioner. Faced with the mounting evidence of
discontent, the respondent apologized for his shortsightedness and agreed that
the family should indeed go overseas on mission work and put space between his
immediate family and extended family. These promises encouraged the petitioner.

[
43
]
To go to Niger, a French speaking
country, required that the petitioner and respondent study French. SIM required
that the petitioner and respondent also complete a year of Bible study to
qualify for mission work under the aegis of SIM. The petitioner, respondent and
children moved to Indianapolis taking up temporary residence with the
petitioner
’
s parents while they attending a nearby Bible College. To appease the
respondent
’
s fears, the petitioner signed a contract agreeing that if the parties
were to divorce they would attorn to the jurisdiction of the Saskatchewan
courts.

[
44
]
It is unnecessary to recount all of the
evidence given by the petitioner and respondent as to how the year in
Indianapolis was spent. Bianca was enrolled in Fox Hill School to which she
adjusted quickly. Sophia warmed up to Grandma and Grandpa USA. After several
trials with various Churches, the petitioner and respondent found their own
respective Churches. The respondent gravitated to a Mennonite congregation and
became heavily involved in that church
’
s youth program, AWANA. He was
previously associated with that program as a leader as much as he continues to
be so to this date. The petitioner gravitated to her parents
’
Church
—
St. Luke
’
s Methodist United. The girls were
exposed to both congregations. The petitioner and respondent were immersed in
religious studies and were devout in their pursuit of Christianity.

[
45
]
Knowing that the marriage was in
difficulty, the petitioner and respondent postured in their respective parental
roles, engaging and vying for dominance during the 11 month stint in
Indianapolis (August 2010 to July 2011). While studying with a view to going
and doing missionary work as a means of healing their marriage, the petitioner
and respondent
’
s communications were failing. Mistrust was permeating their confidence
and relations, perhaps more than either cared to admit. They pursued further
marriage counselling in Indianapolis.

[
46
]
The petitioner related in her testimony
that after completing the year of Bible studies, the petitioner and respondent
contemplated a move to Sherbrooke, Quebec where they would hone their French
speaking skills.

[
47
]
The petitioner returned to Swift
Current in May 2011, ahead of the respondent and girls. In her personal
interviews with the SIM organization the petitioner expressed the view that
homosexuality was not sinful. SIM policy was to the contrary. The petitioner
was therefore deemed unfit to participate in the Niger mission. The petitioner
urged the respondent to still proceed with the move to Sherbrooke. However, the
respondent testified that he could see the writing on the wall and was
therefore unwilling to consider any move away from Swift Current. The
petitioner felt betrayed by the respondent and filed for divorce days after
separating from the respondent,
circa
August 6, 2011.

[
48
]
Since their separation, the petitioner
and respondent have lived under the same roof within the family home. They have
separate bedrooms and live a bifurcated existence. In the Custody Access
Assessment, at p. 52, Mr. Stewart comments as follows:

These current arrangements are
not working very well, as there seems to be a significant amount of tension in
the home. Both children are aware of this tension, and they expressed some
discomfort surrounding the arguments that their parents engage in over the
parenting arrangements that should be in place for the children. Both parents
desire to enter into a joint custody arrangement for the care and upbringing of
Bianca and Sophia. It is Tara
’
s desire to
move to Indianapolis with the children and provide fairly liberal access to
Korvin. Korvin desires to have the children remain in Swift Current, while providing
fairly liberal access to Tara. ...

[
49
]
An earlier quote from the same
assessment is important to also note. At p. 23 Mr. Stewart is discussing the
scores which Tara and Korvin attained in the Parenting Stress Index. At p. 20
Mr. Stewart states:

The Parenting Stress Index
(PSI; 3
rd
Edition) is based on the
“
goodness of fit
”
model and assesses interactions between a child
’
s temperamental characteristics and family variables
that affect parenting ability. Goodness of fit results when a child
’
s capacities, motivations and style of behaving are in
accord with the demands and expectations of the family environment, which then
results in the child
’
s optimal development. Conversely,
“
poorness of fit
”
between
a child and his/her environment results in maladaptive functioning, and
distorted development may occur. So, the test
’
s primary value lies in it
’
s
(sic) ability to identify parent-child symptoms that are under stress and at
risk for the development of dysfunctional parenting problems. The factors
assessed are directly related to the parent
’
s
ability to function as an effective, competent caregiver, while providing a
measure of the quality of interaction between parent and child. Tara and Korvin
were asked to complete two PSI tests each; the first to describe their
parenting relationship with Bianca, and the second to describe their parenting
relationship with Sophia.

[
50
]
Hence, at p. 23 when reviewing Korvin
’
s PSI-3 results regarding Bianca and
Sophia, Mr. Stewart observed as follows:

Within the Parenting Domain,
Korvin obtained scores that ranged from the low-average to the high-average
range. Korvin
’
s scores here indicated that he perceives himself to
be a very competent parent with above-average knowledge of child development
and a wide range of child management skills. Korvin also reported that a high
level of attachment exists between himself and his two children, and he
reported having a healthy degree of freedom while being able to maintain his
role as a parent. That is, Korvin has been able to maintain his own unique
lifestyle and sense of freedom, and does not feel a sense of control or
restriction due to his children
’
s demands or
needs. Korvin
’
s scores within the Parenting Domain also suggested
that he has an average level of support available to him to assist during times
of parenting difficulties or stress. Where Tara obtained average scores on the
“
Spouse
”
sub-scale on
both administrations of the PSI-3, Korvin obtained high average scores on this
scale (70
th
and 75
th
percentile respectively regarding
Bianca and Sophia). Generally, his scores here suggest that Korvin believes
that he does not have as much emotional and active support from Tara in the
area of child management and care when parenting his two daughters, and he is
likely experiencing some negativity in his relationship with Tara. His
high-average scores also suggested that he may be anticipating some
difficulties when he and Tara attempt to be cooperative and supportive in
jointly meeting their childcare responsibilities. It is important to note that
his elevations on this scale was not significantly elevated, but his
high-average scores at the 70
th
and 75
th
percentile does
suggest that co-parenting of Bianca and Sophia may not run as smoothly as Tara
believes (according to her results on this scale).

[
51
]
When interviewing Bianca, the child
responded with the following comment found at p. 35:

I wish my dad
...

Wouldn
’
t fight with mom as much as he does. I hear them fight
quite a bit, usually after we go to bed. I lay in bed and hear them.
Apparently, I don
’
t get to sleep as fast as they think I do (Bianca
gives the writer a coy smile).

[Emphasis in Original]

[
52
]
The Custody Access Assessment is
substantive and may be viewed on the court file at the Local Registrar
’
s office. I will refer to the test
results and assessor
’
s observations later in this judgment. Therefore, the quotes
in the preceding paragraphs emphasize the environment for parenting since the
date of separation, with the parents living under one roof was problematic.
Those quotes should be considered in their context. The point which is obvious
and must be made is that the petitioner seeks to leave the family home when
judgment is rendered. To the contrary, the respondent clings to a naive and
untenable view that he and the petitioner could successfully coexist in the
home if the children and petitioner remain in Swift Current. I find as fact
that the children are being adversely affected by the strained relationship in
the family home. They are quoted in the assessment at some length and are quite
aware of their parents fighting behind closed doors. They are more observant of
their parents behavior and moods than the parents give them credit for. The
children
’
s best interests require intervention
and regrettably, the petitioner and respondent cannot resolve the issue of
primary parenting and residency, deferring to the court to make such a decision
for them.

[
53
]
The petitioner and respondent took
great pains and time during the trial to explain in detail, sometimes bordering
upon minutia, how each of them parents Bianca and Sophia. Each believes their
different parenting styles is superior to the other. The respondent says the
petitioner is too permissive. The petitioner says the respondent is too
authoritarian (not authoritative), that he is too strict and prone to yelling
and spanking the girls. The respondent says the petitioner is self-absorbed in
her physical workouts and professional interests to the girls
’
detriment. The petitioner says the
respondent does not have the girls
’
attachment, confidence and affinity
as does the petitioner enjoy.

[
54
]
Mr. Stewart concludes that each parent
has a different parenting style and personality. But he concludes with the
opinion that both would be loving and adequate caregivers. However, Mr. Stewart
does conclude that the weight of results of the psychometric testing combined
with the interviews of the key players, the petitioner, respondent and
children, leads him to conclude that the children
’
s best interests are to be best
served or attained if the petitioner is designated the primary parent. Such
conclusion stops short of the proposed relocation of the children, which as I
stated earlier is a matter which Mr. Stewart says is for the court to decide,
and not himself.

[
55
]
The petitioner, as well as the
respondent, described their children to the court. Bianca is 8
½

judgment. I find that the best interests of Bianca and Sophia will be served by
being in their mother
’
s primary care. To this end, neither the respondent nor his
family shall have any status to interfere with the petitioner
’
s private life, her home life,
professional life or parenting of the girls. The petitioner
’
s social life shall be as a femme
sole. Thus, her main complaints and concerns are addressed. In matters of the
girls
’
grooming, dress and health care
issues, the petitioner shall have exclusive authority over these parenting
matters.

[
191
]
The petitioner and respondent shall
continue as joint legal custodians of Bianca and Sophia. There is no
evidentiary basis nor reason to disenfranchise one parent and to legally
empower the other as a sole custodian.

[
192
]
My basis for continuing joint custody
follows the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal
’
s
decision in
Schick v. Woodrow
,

2012 SKCA 1
,
385 Sask. R. 153
. At paras. 24 and 25, the court states the
following:

[24]          These
considerations, on the other hand, cannot in themselves be determinative where
the non‑resident parent seeks standing as a joint legal custodian, with
joint decision making power and authority, and regular access to the child, as
distinct from de facto custody, or primary residence of the child. This, I
think, is the issue addressed by McIntyre J. in
B.O.A. v. R.G.
,
2003
SKQB 112
,
38 R.F.L. (5th) 367
, where he held that it was not in the best
interests of the child that one parent should be "a passive
bystander," where that parent has bonded with the child, and demonstrated
love and care for the child.

[25]          I agree with this
point. In my view, even where one parent has been designated the parent of
primary residence, it is presumptively in the best interests of a child to have
as much contact with each parent as is reasonably possible having regard to the
given circumstances and for each parent to play as active a role in the life of
the child as is practical. There is significant risk that a parent who is
prevented from playing such a role and becomes a passive bystander in the
child's life will eventually drift away from on‑going involvement in the
child's life. These considerations favour an order for joint custody in the
absence of some reason relevant to the best interest of the child to the
contrary. Examples of reasons to the contrary might include an insurmountable
inability of the parents to communicate sufficiently well to be able to make
important and necessary decisions regarding the child, or evidence of
indifference or of inappropriate or abusive behaviour on the part of the parent
who does not have primary care of the child. No such reasons were cited or are
evidence in this case.

[
193
]
All major decisions regarding educating
the girls can be a collaborative effort between the petitioner and respondent.
The girls should continue to attend the same school and remain in the french
immersion program if that is the common desire of the girls and parents. I find
the french immersion argument more relevant to preparing the girls for the
prospect of living in a french speaking country like Niger
–
a prospect which no longer exists.

[
194
]
The children must have a considerable
voice in choosing the extracurricular activities they wish to engage in. The
petitioner and respondent should be mindful of the children
’
s wishes and their aptitudes in
regards to their choices. I find no evidence before me to suggest the choice of
and management of the children
’
s extracurricular activities will be problematic for the
petitioner and respondent. The parent caring for the girls at the time the
activity occurs shall have the primary responsibility to facilitate the child
’
s attendance. Both parents may attend
such public activities and events in which either child is participating.

[
195
]
To ensure maximum contact and thereby
achieve a parenting scheme which augers with the best interests of Bianca and
Sophia, the respondent shall parent the children between the end of the school
day on Thursday until the commencement of school the following Monday morning
in each alternate week. Then, on the Wednesday evening preceding the petitioner
’
s weekend, the respondent shall parent
Bianca and Sophia from the time school recesses until 9:00 p.m. I have chosen
Wednesday as the evening when AWANA is held. If AWANA is on another week day
evening of the week preceding the mother
’
s weekend, that evening shall
substitute for Wednesday. In this manner, the children will have the maximum
weekly contact with the respondent as befits their best interests. A move to
Indianapolis would have seriously jeopardized the girls
’
relationship with their father and
offend the maximum contact principle for no justifiable reason.

[
196
]
The holidays which involve school breaks,
Christmas, spring break, Easter and summer recess shall be divided equally
between the petitioner and respondent. To date, I am confident that no more
detailed direction is required for the parties. However, they are to agree to
the dates for division of such school holidays no less than 14 days prior to
the commencement of each holiday. If they fail to achieve an agreement in any
instance, they may apply to the court in the regular fashion.

[
197
]
Father
’
s day and Mother
’
s day shall be recognized with Bianca
and Sophia being with the celebrant parent from at least 9:00 a.m. until 8:00
p.m., irrespective of the regular parenting schedule.

[
198
]
The petitioner and respondent shall each
have no less than two exclusive hours with Bianca and Sophia on the child
’
s respective birthday.

[
199
]
The petitioner and respondent are free to
deviate from this judgment by mutual agreement. If they choose to do so, it may
be wise to sign a simple letter or note setting forth their mutual
understanding in each instance.

Religious
Instruction

[
200
]
The petitioner and respondent have
demonstrated in their evidence that they are devout Christians, though of
different denominations. As a matter of pursuing a child
’
s best interests, it is consonant
that Bianca and Sophia be exposed to the faith of each parent. This includes
education and participation in each parent
’
s Church life. However, the best
interests principle also dictates that such education and participation must be
reasonable and in moderation. In due course, the children will approach
adolescence and be free to pursue their faith of choice. There is no evidence
before the court to constrain either the petitioner nor respondent in sharing
their respective faiths with their children.

[
201
]
Canadian law has long since recognized
that engaging children in religious practices of the faith of either parent is
appropriate so long as the exposure is not detrimental to the best interests of
the child.
See
Young v. Young,

1993 CanLII 34 (SCC)
,
[1993] 4 S.C.R. 3
. At p.11, the Court
states:

... Decisions regarding custody
and access must not be based on the parents' faith, whether or not that
religion is that of the majority. However, the religion of the parties may be
relevant as one of the circumstances to be assessed along with all the others
in the determination of the best interests of the child, as it is in this case.

[
202
]
At p. 100, the Court further states:

The best interests of the child
must be approached from a child‑centred perspective. It is not simply the
right to be free of significant harm. It is the right of the particular child
in question to the best possible arrangements in the circumstances of the
parties, taking into consideration the wide spectrum of factors which may
affect the child's physical, spiritual, moral and emotional well‑being
and the milieu in which the child lives.

[
203
]
The head note from
Young, supra
,
contains another paragraph which I consider highly instructive:

Ordinarily, the exposure of a
child to different religions or beliefs may be of value to the child. Where
religion becomes a source of conflict between the parents or is the very cause
of the marriage breakdown, it is generally not in the best interests of the
child and may in some circumstances be very detrimental for the child to be
drawn into the controversy over religious matters. Where there is conflict over
religion, courts must secure the longstanding authority of the custodial parent
to make decisions over religious activities. This ensures that stress
occasioned by such issues does not become a continuing and ultimately
destructive feature in the life of the child after divorce.

Education
of the Girls

[
204
]
As to the education of Bianca and Sophia,
the court is mindful of the inherent difficulty with the petitioner and
respondent
’
s relationship which has encompassed competing for control and authority
over the children
’
s lives.

[
205
]

Subsection 6(1)
(c) of
The
Children
’
s Law Act, 1997
allows the court to,
“
make any additional order that the
court considers necessary and proper in the circumstances
”
. Under this authority, and given the
competitive nature of the respondent, I order that the petitioner consult with
the respondent beforehand in making any major decision relevant to the

’
s discretion as the primary parent
shall prevail.

[
206
]

Subsection 9(2)
of
The
Children
’
s Law Act, 1997
is often overlooked. It provides:

9.
(2)        Unless otherwise ordered by the court, a
parent who is granted access to a child has the same right as the custodial
parent to make inquiries and be given information concerning the health,
education and welfare of the child.

This
statutory right is certainly applicable where joint custody is continued and
the court designates one of the parents as the primary caregiver. My foregoing
order as to the education of the girls is subject to
ss. 9(2)
and is not to be
construed as derogating from the respondent
’
s rights as set for in
ss. 9(2)
.

[
207
]
Having dismissed the petitioner
’
s application to relocate the children
to Indianapolis, it is necessary to order that the petitioner give the
respondent at least 30 day
’
s advance notice or such other notice as the court may
specify. To be practical and mindful of the time required to challenge and
bring a variation application to the court, I direct that the petitioner given
the respondent no less than 60 day
’
s advance written notice of any
intention on her part to relocate the children
’
s residence in the future (
ss.
6(5)
(b) of
The
Children
’
s Law Act, 1997)
.

[
208
]
For the petitioner and respondent
’
s edification, designation of the
petitioner as primary parent gives the petitioner authority over the day-to-day
management of the children
’
s lives
–
that is, the limitless number of minor decisions required of
a parent in the day-to-day management and lives of the children. The petitioner
is not to misconstrue her authority as that of a sole custodial parent.

[
209
]
There are a number of arguments adduced
by the petitioner and respondent at trial which I acknowledge but do not find,
of themselves, highly probative. One is the matter of the respondent
’
s admitted addiction to pornography.
Given the paucity of evidence explaining what each witness (the petitioner,
respondent and respondent
’
s pastor) meant by using the word
“
pornography
”
and any attempt to explain or
elaborate upon the nature of the pornography to which the respondent was

in the respondent
’
s parenting of the girls. However, I am required to leave it

’
s addiction to pornography lies within that spectrum.

[
210
]
Given the freedom and independence which
will come with divorce and this judgment, the petitioner
’
s real concerns over control and
intrusion into her private life, as well as professional limitations, are
addressed and rectified. The other reasons advanced by the petitioner are based
upon her quest for personal happiness and advancement. None of those reasons
are sufficient, viewed separately nor in the cumulative, to outweigh the best
interests of the children and maintaining the maximum contact with their
father, extended family, personal friends or community.

[
211
]
The maternal grandparents are retired
persons of sufficient means to visit Swift Current. The petitioner is likewise

overarching principle of determining where the best interests of Bianca and

judgment.
